title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training-data provenance: an AI music generation system was built using copyrighted recordings without the rights holders' authorization. This is a data-acquisition problem that occurs before deployment, at the point where decisions are made about what material to include in a training corpus. The legal disputes that followed involve multiple major labels and independent artists, all alleging that their recordings were used without permission. A licensing review of training data before model development began would have been the point at which this could have been caught.

The incident sits at the intersection of a known structural gap in generative AI development, where the cost and complexity of clearing rights leads some developers to train on uncleared material. The settlement between Udio and some labels, under which a future platform would use only authorized music, implicitly acknowledges that the original training corpus did not meet that standard. The separate class action by independent artists, which a court declined to dismiss, indicates the exposure extends beyond major-label catalogues.

What is not established is whether any court has found Udio liable for copyright infringement, whether the financial terms of any settlement include admissions of wrongdoing, or whether the specific training practices alleged by Sony constitute infringement as a legal matter. Lawsuits and settlements are not findings, and the allegations remain unresolved in several active proceedings.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group and AI music startup Udio have settled a lawsuit by reaching licensing agreements. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, including The Temptations' "My Girl." Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, stream, and share songs. The financial terms were not disclosed. UMG chairman Lucian Grainge stated the agreements demonstrate the label's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies and developing new business models.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, allows users to create original music from text prompts using AI. The company has attracted millions of users since its launch and counts music artist will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz among its backers. This marks Udio's first licensing deal with a major music label. The company stated that artists can opt into the new platform and will receive compensation, though specific details were not provided.
